For here, as in many other places, whatever profit is collected returns entirely to the King. Bordering this place are the workshops of the goldsmiths, whose consul <note>a guild leader or presiding official</note> keeps the seal and the dies for the coins. In Fez <term>Fessa</term> <gloss>the city of Fez, Morocco</gloss>, neither a ring nor any other object may be manufactured from gold or silver unless the metal has first been stamped with a seal; for they punish transgressors most severely. But once the metal is sealed, whatever is made from it is weighed out as if it were currency. The greatest part of the goldsmiths who inhabit New Fez <term>Fessam novam</term> <gloss>Fez el-Jdid, the administrative city founded in the 13th century</gloss> consists of Jews, and they carry gold and silver vessels to Old Fez <term>Fessam antiquam</term> <gloss>Fez el-Bali, the original city center</gloss> to a certain place situated not far from the spice merchants and sell them. For in Old Fez, neither gold nor silver is minted, nor is it permitted for Muslims to practice that craft, because they have usurers <note>original: "fœneratores"; this refers to the religious prohibition against selling precious metal items for more than their weight value, which was categorized as usury</note> who resell a piece of silver or gold work at a higher price than its weight warrants, although this is permitted to the Jews by the city governors. You may also find here some who manufacture vessels only for the citizens, to whom payment is counted out only in proportion to the value of their labor.
